why: Three files, 1120 lines, and they are not one job but two. wa_decrypt.py (213 lines) reimplements the WhatsApp Desktop WebView2 key chain in Python: ODUID from clipc.dll, staticKey via DPAPI-NG NCryptProtectSecret (LOCAL=user), clientKey carved from session.db-wal with sha1(clientKey) asserted against the session directory name, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 plus AES-256-CBC to the nativeSettings key, then per-type keys over AES-OFB page-encrypted SQLite. wa_query.py (178 lines) is the part no prior art supplies: a contacts/stats/search/thread CLI over the decrypted store with name resolution and date filters, output shaped for an agent to quote from. wa_act.py (729 lines, two thirds of the component) is a different thing again, a CDP driver against live WhatsApp Web that exists because the decrypted linked-device store has no from-me flag and cannot attribute a line to a speaker. The decryption is genuinely prior art and this record says so; the CORPUS QUERY is what is not available anywhere as a tool, and that is a 178-line file. The honest reading of the size is that the component is 549 lines of automation wrapped around 178 lines of the actual capability.
what_ours_does: Decrypts to a local temp directory on a snapshot copy without touching the live store, works while WhatsApp is running via shared-mode reads, resolves chatIds to contact names, and answers a question with dated quotes plus a stated coverage window rather than a dump. States its own epistemic limits in SKILL.md: no sender direction in the store, no media, group prefixes only on @g.us, coverage is what the linked device synced.
strongest_counterargument: ZAPiXDESK already does the decryption, it was published first, it is GPLv3, it is the source this reimplementation cites, and it does one thing ours does not: it hashes the extraction for chain of custody. Reimplementing a published forensic technique in a second language is the textbook case of code that should have been a dependency. The counterargument goes further than the code: the ONLY reason the query half exists at all is that the decrypted output is a raw SQLite file, and a raw SQLite file is already queryable by sqlite3, so `wa_query.py` is arguably 178 lines of convenience over four SQL statements. Against that: ZAPiXDESK is a PowerShell script with C# and Bouncy Castle that produces a ZIP for a forensic suite to open, its stated dependency is possessing the ODUID, and it has no query surface at all. Shelling out to it would mean adding a .NET crypto dependency and a ZIP unpack step to get to the same SQLite file, on a machine where the Python path already works. That is a defensible reason to keep the 213 lines and a WEAK reason to keep the other 907. If wa_act.py were split out to its own component, this record's verdict would be closer to a coin flip.

alternatives.name: ZAPiXDESK (kraftdenker / Alberto Magno)
alternatives.why_not: The closest prior art by a wide margin and the acknowledged source of the technique, cited in our own SKILL.md. It targets both WebView2 and legacy UWP builds, extracts the ODUID live, decrypts every LocalState db and WAL, and emits a ZIP with an MD5 for chain of custody, which is a capability ours lacks. Rejected as a dependency rather than as a technique: it is PowerShell plus C# over Bouncy Castle producing an archive for a forensic tool to open, and it never queries what it decrypts. Adopting it swaps a stdlib-plus-cryptography Python path for a .NET toolchain, and still leaves the entire query surface to build. Its MD5 manifest is worth stealing and is not in improvement_owed only because chain of custody is not this use case.

alternatives.name: Kim, Hur, Kang and Kim, 'Analyzing the Web and UWP versions of WhatsApp for digital forensics', FSI: Digital Investigation v52 (2025), art. 301861
alternatives.why_not: Not a tool, and listed because the record would be dishonest without it: this is the peer-reviewed reverse engineering the implementation stands on, covering WhatsApp Web v2.3000.x and UWP v2.2421.7.0 on Windows. A paper cannot be adopted, only implemented, which is what happened. Its relevance to the verdict is the reverse of an alternative: it means the key chain is published, will drift when WhatsApp changes it, and our 213 lines will need re-deriving from the next paper rather than from our own analysis. The publication also caps any novelty claim about the decryption to zero.

alternatives.name: WhatsApp-Chat-Exporter (KnugiHK)
alternatives.why_not: The mature, maintained, cross-platform parser: Android msgstore including crypt12/14/15, iOS/iPadOS iTunes backups, HTML/JSON/text output, call logs, contacts, media organisation. It is better than ours at everything it covers, and it explicitly does not cover WhatsApp Desktop or Windows, which is the only store on this machine. Correct choice the day the operator wants the phone backup parsed; useless for the store that is actually here.

alternatives.name: Magnet AXIOM
alternatives.why_not: Industry-leading artifact coverage across mobile, computer, cloud and vehicle, with timeline analysis and reporting that would outclass any hand-rolled query. Rejected on shape and cost, not quality: it is a licensed investigator workstation aimed at law enforcement, federal and enterprise IR, priced accordingly, and its output is a case file and a report rather than a CLI an agent can call in a loop. Nothing in it is packageable into a skill that answers 'what did X say about Y in August' inside a session.

alternatives.name: Belkasoft X Forensic
alternatives.why_not: Cheaper than AXIOM and perpetually licensed rather than term-based, which removes the usual objection to a commercial suite. Rejected for a specific reason found while reading it: its product page advertises WhatsApp support as cloud acquisition, backup download and QR-code chat download, and does not state WhatsApp DESKTOP WebView2 artifact support. The one capability needed is the one not confirmed, and buying a suite to find out is not a plan. Recheck this claim before any future purchase argument, since suite artifact coverage changes per release.

alternatives.name: The official WhatsApp Export Chat feature
alternatives.why_not: The simplest correct option and the one this record is obliged to compare against, since it needs no decryption, no reverse engineering and no maintenance. It is per-chat and manual, which is the disqualifier: the corpus question here spans every thread at once, and hand-exporting hundreds of chats to text files is not a corpus, it is a chore with a different failure mode. WhatsApp's own privacy policy confirms the relevant fact that makes the local path viable at all: messages are stored on the device and not typically on their servers, so there is no server-side archive to request instead.

alternatives.name: sqlite3 against the decrypted file, with no query layer at all
alternatives.why_not: The other simplest option, and it is half-right. Once wa_decrypt.py has run, the store is an ordinary SQLite database and `message(rowid, id, chatId, timestamp, text)` is four joins away from every answer wa_query.py gives. What the 178 lines buy is name resolution (a chatId such as 53403707257078@lid is not a person), the busiest-thread tie-break on ambiguous names, and a fixed output shape that keeps other people's messages from being dumped wholesale into a model's context. That last one is a policy control, not a convenience, which is why the layer stays.

improvement_owed: It leaves the entire decrypted corpus on disk and nothing removes it. wa_decrypt.py's main() creates %LOCALAPPDATA%/Temp/wa-decrypted, writes genericStorage.dec.db, contacts.dec.db and their WALs, prints 'do not commit or share it', and exits. There is no cleanup path anywhere in the component: `rmtree`, `unlink` and `tempfile` appear nowhere in the file, and the only import of shutil is for the snapshot copy. So a single query leaves an unencrypted plaintext mirror of every message the operator has, indefinitely, in a world-readable-by-this-user temp directory, protected by nothing. That is strictly worse than the state WhatsApp ships, which is why it is the first thing owed: a context manager that decrypts, answers, and deletes, or at minimum a --purge verb and a wa_query exit that removes the mirror it caused to exist. ZAPiXDESK's extraction hash is worth adopting at the same time. Second, ours has no selftest and no mutation entry, so a WhatsApp key-chain change would be discovered by a query failing in front of the operator rather than by a check.

evidence.runs_today: no. `python dot-claude/skills/whatsapp-query/wa_query.py contacts --limit 3` exits with 'messages DB not found: C:\\Users\\shova\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\wa-decrypted\\genericStorage.dec.db. Run wa_decrypt.py first.'
evidence.mirror_note: The 86.9 MB plaintext mirror measured twice earlier in this session is NOT on disk at 2026-07-31 review time; the directory does not exist. It was removed out of band, not by this component. The defect is unchanged and is about the code, not the current directory listing: nothing in the component deletes what it writes, so the next decrypt recreates the exposure.
evidence.integrity_check_present: yes, sha1(clientKey) is asserted against the session directory name and warns on mismatch
evidence.selftest: none; the component has no oracle and no entry in tools/audit/mutate.py

recheck: Two things flip this verdict. First, if the cleanup defect is still unfixed at recheck, the verdict should move to replace-or-delete: a tool that silently creates a permanent unencrypted copy of every message the operator has is worse than not having the tool, and no query convenience outweighs that. Second, re-check whether WhatsApp Desktop has changed its key chain (a decrypt failure is the signal), and whether ZAPiXDESK or WhatsApp-Chat-Exporter has grown a Python-callable Windows-desktop path; either would make the 213-line decryptor a dependency instead of an asset. Also verify the Belkasoft X desktop-artifact question against its then-current release notes rather than against this record.
